source: Shah, Smith, Vargas-Hernandez (2003) Metrics for measuring ideation effectiveness
finding: Founding paper. Proposes four effectiveness measures for idea generation: quantity, quality, novelty, variety. Novelty and variety are scored against a genealogy tree of the idea set. The paper itself could not be opened (publisher blocked); this line is from background knowledge and from papers that cite it.
numbers: Semantic Scholar metadata page opened: 1159 citations (2026). The four metrics are named in the Sankar and Sen CAI paper (a11).
limits: Formula details not verified; full text not read this session.
agent_relevance: Gives the minimum set of what to measure for an ideation step: count, spread, rarity, quality. Our agent trace can record all four per run.

source: Shah, Smith, Vargas-Hernandez (2003): variety and novelty scoring detail
finding: Variety is scored by how far apart ideas sit on the genealogy tree: levels run from physical principle down through working principle and embodiment to detail, with higher weights for higher levels. Novelty has an a-priori form (against the field) and an a-posteriori form (against the idea set the group produced).
numbers: From memory: level weights about 10, 6, 3, 1 for the four tree levels. NOT verified in this session.
limits: Unverified numbers. Check against the paper before use.
agent_relevance: A-posteriori novelty (rarity inside the sample) needs no human expert, so an automated agent can compute it. The embedding-distance metrics in a12 and a13 descend from it.

source: Shah, Kulkarni, Vargas-Hernandez (2000) Evaluation of idea generation methods for conceptual design
url: n/a (seen only in the reference list of arXiv 2409.07578)
finding: Earlier ASME paper cited in the Sankar and Sen reference list. It compared idea generation methods with effectiveness measures that became the 2003 metrics.
numbers: Reference line only; no numbers read.
limits: Reference only; not opened.
agent_relevance: Method comparisons by measured spread and count are the template for testing scaffold operators.

source: Fiorineschi and Rotini (2023) Uses of the novelty metrics proposed by Shah et al.: what emerges from the literature?
finding: Literature review of how the Shah novelty metrics are used. Publisher page and PDF returned HTTP 503 or empty. Only the title and citation metadata were seen (14 citations). Two papers I did read (a12, a13) cite it for the point that novelty and diversity are usually computed as distance from a reference set.
numbers: Title and 14 citations only.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A whole review literature exists on how to use the metric; open it in a follow-up pass.

source: Fiorineschi et al. (2019 to 2021) variants of Shah's a-posteriori novelty metric (three papers)
finding: Search metadata lists a series: 'Orienting through the Variants of the Shah's A-Posteriori Novelty Metric' (2019), 'Impact of missing attributes on the novelty metric of Shah et al.' (2020, Research in Engineering Design), 'Refined metric for a-posteriori novelty assessments' (2021, J Engineering Design). Titles suggest the score changes when attributes are missing or weighted differently.
numbers: Titles only. Citation counts seen: 8, 23, 12.
limits: None opened. Direction of effects not checked.
agent_relevance: A metric score depends on the chosen attribute list. Any agent metric needs a fixed, logged feature set.

source: Egea et al. (2024) ChatGPT as an inventor: strengths and weaknesses of LLMs against humans in engineering design
finding: 48-hour Nerf-dart launcher hackathon. One team was fully directed by ChatGPT 4.0 (two humans executed its instructions). It ranked 2nd of 6. It prototyped all three main concepts seen across teams (pneumatic, spring, elastic) but none outside them. It dropped the pneumatic concept after one iteration when the valves did not fit. Authors report design fixation on details in prompts.
numbers: 116 prototypes; chat of 97 prompts. Final dart distance: 37 m (winning human team), 14.8 m (ChatGPT team), 8.1, 6.6, 5.1, 0.1 m.
quote: tends to go with the "safe" solution rather than taking a risk on an unorthodox idea
limits: One run, one LLM, one task: n=1 LLM team. Chat coded by one author. GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 were mixed within the run.
agent_relevance: Process metrics (prototype count, concept switches) matter alongside idea lists. The LLM chose the safe concept set and quit on the first setback: supports doubt-on-signal (G1) plus a persistence rule.

source: Egea et al. (2024): chat-log coding scheme
finding: The chat log was coded into six categories: idea generation, feedback and iteration, instructions, questions, decision making, problem solving. The categories were first proposed by ChatGPT itself, then checked by the authors.
numbers: 6 codes; 97 prompt-response pairs; one coder.
limits: Single coder; no inter-rater reliability in the text I read. LLM-proposed codes may lean toward LLM-like categories.
agent_relevance: A cheap process metric: share of turns spent generating versus iterating. Code can compute it from the agent trace.

source: Anderson, Shah, Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of LLMs on human creative ideation (C&C 24)
finding: Within-subject study: ChatGPT versus an Oblique Strategies card deck as idea tool. Each person's own ideas were no less varied with ChatGPT, but ideas were more alike across people. Fluency, flexibility and elaboration rose.
numbers: 36 recruited, 33 analysed (df=32). Group-level distance from mean embedding: 0.24 (SD .07) ChatGPT vs 0.28 (SD .08), t=2.154, p=.038, d=.47. Individual-level: .65 vs .66, p=.352. Ideas per prompt: 8.39 vs 7.32, p=.044, d=.32 (about +15%). Categories hit: 8.58 vs 6.77, p=.001, d=.54 (+27%). Elaboration words 8.25 vs 6.46. 181 idea categories from 1271 responses.
limits: Small sample; ChatGPT 3.5 only; the comparison was a card deck, not a no-tool control; embeddings not validated for creativity beforehand (authors ran a small check).
agent_relevance: Pattern to measure: individual spread holds or rises, population spread falls. Our agent should measure spread across independent runs, not only inside one run (G4).

source: Wan and Kalman (2025) Diverse AI personas can mitigate the homogenization effect in human-AI collaborative ideation
finding: Extension and partial replication of Doshi and Hauser (2024). Their modified design did not reproduce the original homogenisation: with plots from ten diverse AI personas, story similarity did not rise versus the human-only baseline.
numbers: 300 persona plots; intra-persona similarity 87.41 (SD 3.17) vs inter-persona 82.93 (SD 3.12), difference 4.49, t=119.94, Cohen d=1.43. Human phase: 100 Prolific participants, 97 kept. 1-plot b=-0.493 p=.301; 5-plot b=-0.356 p=.459; ANOVA F(2,94)=0.573 p=.57. Original reported 0.871 and 0.718 on the same scale (significant). Doshi and Hauser: similarity up 10.7% (1 plot) and 8.9% (5 plots).
limits: Authors' own power estimate: 55.4% to detect the observed effect size (f=0.244), versus 96.9% for the original. So the null is weak evidence. Prompt design was modified.
agent_relevance: A weak or failed replication plus a practical lever: vary the generating persona. Note G4: personas help spread of ideas, not independence of votes on one answer.

source: Dong and Yakura (2026) Human diversity fuels collective creativity that LLMs cannot simulate or sustain
finding: Preregistered metaphor experiment with native (L1) and non-native (L2) English writers. AI-supplied ideas compressed collective diversity; AI used only to refine the writer's own ideas did not. LLM-simulated writer pools (persona prompts, three model families, higher temperature) fell below every human pool.
numbers: L1 n=318, L2 n=326; 351 evaluators. Centroid similarity (lower = more diverse): human-only L1 0.421 vs L2 0.398 (p=.003); AI ideation L1 0.457 vs L2 0.451 (p=.481). AI ideation vs human-only b=0.036, p<.001; AI refinement b=0.007, p=.516. 84 of 228 L2 writers (37%) used their native language with AI: 0.442 (L1), 0.427 (L2 English), 0.421 (L2 native), linear contrast p=.015.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Metaphors, not engineering concepts. Simulation part not preregistered.
agent_relevance: Where the model enters the workflow decides spread: model as generator shrinks it, model as editor does not.

source: Sankar and Sen (2024) A novel idea generation tool using a structured conversational AI system
finding: Compares 20-minute traditional ideation (brainstorming, SCAMPER and others) with a GPT-based ideation tool, using Shah's terms (quantity, novelty, variety). GPT arm gave about three times the ideas and higher expert ratings for novelty and variety.
numbers: Six problem statements, groups of five designers. Ideas per 20 min: 4.8 traditional vs 15 CAI. Novelty rating (1 to 5, 80 expert raters): 2.5 vs 3.86. Variety rating: 2.9 vs 4.2. 20 expert product designers judged GPT ideas more meaningful: 68%.
limits: Pilot. Raters likely saw longer, more polished GPT text; no inter-rater statistics seen; no length control; variety rated on a random 12-idea subset rather than computed from a tree.
agent_relevance: Typical positive LLM result and the weak side of the evidence: ratings may track length and polish (G5 verbosity warning).

source: Sankar and Sen (2025) A novel mathematical framework for objective characterization of ideas
finding: Replaces human novelty and variety ratings with text embeddings plus UMAP and DBSCAN clustering. Lists metric families: individual quality (novelty, originality, creativity), population quality (diversity, quantity), relevance (usefulness, feasibility). Argues human rating is slow, noisy and mixes constructs.
numbers: Six idea sets of 100 ideas each. 40 graduate design students picked 10 of 100 points from cluster maps: Sampling Score SS=1 in 3 of 6 plots, near 1 in 2 more, low in idea set 4 (3 sparse clusters). Picking took about 2 of the 10 minutes allowed.
limits: No correlation with human ratings found in the sections I read. Selection study used non-experts. Ideas came from one prompt and one temperature.
agent_relevance: A recipe for an automatic variety metric: cluster count and spread of embeddings across the candidate set. Cheap, run by code, no model judge (G5).

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix: evaluation framework for creative defixation prompting in LLMs
finding: Large controlled test of 567 conditions and 25 prompts built on brainstorming, C-K, TRIZ, design thinking, scenarios, SCAMPER and four LLM-specific category-negation prompts. Metrics: fluency, diversity (mean pairwise embedding distance), novelty (distance from control ideas), rarity, overlap, perplexity. Every method prompt beat control, short 'think outside the box' prompts beat long method prompts, and outputs stayed alike across models.
numbers: Five models. Fluency: Gemini 10.43, GPT-4o 12.91, Grok 20.16, Qwen 19.87, Llama-70B 9.35. Diversity .464, .431, .482, .403, .485. Novelty .463, .428, .481, .509, .556 (top-5 .523 to .61). Cross-model pairwise distance only 0.206 to 0.341. Top-5 novelty gains up to about +41% (AI-specific) and +40% (C-K). 3 runs per model; 14,350 prompts.
limits: Embedding distance is a proxy with no human check. Non-iterative. Two control prompts define what counts as common. Effect described by authors as moderate.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that explicit divergence instruction beats elaborate method scaffolds for novelty, and that no prompt fixes cross-model sameness. Measure novelty against a control pool from the same model.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: INFINITY-CHAT: 26K real open-ended queries, 31,250 human annotations. Reports repetition inside a model and strong similarity across models. 15.2% of real queries are brainstorming and ideation.
numbers: 50 responses per query over 100 queries: average same-prompt pairwise similarity typically above 0.8 (top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0). Cross-model similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs Qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs GPT-4o 0.81). Random pairs from the global pool fall in 0.1 to 0.2. Under min-p, 81% of pairs exceed 0.7 and 61.2% exceed 0.8.
limits: Null was unrelated prompts (see a15). No human baseline. Embedding similarity only.
agent_relevance: Shows why samples from one model are not independent (G4) and why spread must be measured, not assumed.

source: Schaeffer et al. (2026) How strong is the evidence for the Artificial Hivemind?
finding: Re-examination of Jiang et al. The flagship 'time metaphor' example is not two clusters; the null (unrelated prompts) is too easy; prompting does raise measured diversity. The authors do not claim the hivemind is false.
numbers: Under a harder null (same prompt, truly different ideas), 20% to 32% of pairs already exceed the 0.8 threshold; different-cluster pairs exceed 0.7 and 0.8 in 61% and 32% of cases (54% and 20% on the other split). Original same-prompt pairs exceed 0.8 about two to three times as often as different-idea pairs. Prompting raised diversity across 12 topics and 15 models.
limits: Preprint; critique of one paper; their own metrics (Rao's Q, modal-idea share) are also embedding based.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for every embedding metric: report a matched null (same prompt, different ideas) or similarity numbers overstate homogeneity.

source: Park et al. (2026) Beyond One Path: MUTATE, divergent thinking in interactive LLM agents
finding: Benchmark scoring agents on path-level divergence (mechanism-distinct paths to one goal) and action-level divergence, not only success. Under pressure to converge, agents fixate on the first action. ReDNA, which separates open candidate generation from later constraint selection, improved results.
numbers: 56 scenarios. Path discovery: GPT-5.4 27/56 (48.2%) to 38/56 (67.9%); Claude Sonnet 4.6 30/56 (53.6%) to 41/56 (73.2%); Llama 4 Maverick 13/56 (23.2%) to 29/56 (51.8%); Qwen3-235B 22/56 (39.3%) to 36/56 (64.3%). Self-Refine on Claude: 25/56, below its base of 30/56.
limits: Constructed scenarios; originality and elaboration scored partly by LLM raters; four models.
agent_relevance: Supports a generate-wide then select-narrow split, and shows self-refine can hurt. A count of distinct paths found is an agent-native variety metric.

source: Doshi and Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces collective diversity (Science Advances)
finding: Seen only through Wan and Kalman (a09) and IDEAFix (a13). Stories written with GenAI plot ideas were rated more creative, but the set of stories was more similar.
numbers: Via a09: cosine similarity up 10.7% (1 idea) and 8.9% (5 ideas); regression coefficients 0.871 and 0.718.
limits: Original not opened. Numbers are second-hand.
agent_relevance: The canonical individual-up, collective-down finding that metric work must separate.

source: Sankar and Sen (2025): comparative evaluation of idea sets
finding: Authors say existing AI novelty methods score each idea alone and so cannot help pick a diverse shortlist; clusters let novices pick 10 diverse ideas out of 100 quickly. Idea sets from six different problems each formed their own island in the combined UMAP plot.
numbers: 10 of 100 ideas chosen in about 2 minutes; SS=1 in 3 of 6 plots.
limits: Claim of outperforming other AI methods rests on figures and discussion, not a reported correlation.
agent_relevance: Set-level scoring (spread of the whole pool) is what a selector needs; per-idea scores alone miss redundancy.

source: Egea et al. (2024): recommendations
finding: Authors give six recommendations: use the LLM for ideation, keep humans on key decisions, iterate on feedback, prompt it to consider alternatives, give specific subsystem tasks, and ask it directly to avoid design fixation.
numbers: No numeric test of the recommendations.
limits: Untested design advice, not measured effects.
agent_relevance: Candidate operator: after a failed attempt, force an alternative from a different working principle before dropping the concept.

source: Anderson et al. (2024): originality measures
finding: Uses Torrance dimensions (fluency, flexibility, elaboration, originality), with originality as embedding distance; avoids rating quality as subjective and costly. Tested uniqueness three ways: ideas nobody else had, categories under 5% of people, frequency-weighted flexibility. None showed a ChatGPT effect.
numbers: Unique ideas 0.74 vs 0.97, p=.108. 5%-threshold categories 0.87 vs 0.90, p=.894. Weighted flexibility 6.34 vs 5.50, p=.164. Authors note uniqueness depends on sample size.
limits: Uniqueness counts are unstable with small samples.
agent_relevance: Rarity counts need a large reference pool. Prefer distance-based scores for small runs.

source: Dong and Yakura (2026): individual rating versus collective diversity
finding: AI ideation raised each writer's own rating while lowering pool diversity, except when L2 writers used their native language. Human raters scored novelty and surprise blind to condition.
numbers: 351 native-English evaluators, 4 items per metaphor; LLM judges tracked each other only moderately (rank agreement reported in the supplement).
limits: Preprint.
agent_relevance: A reward on single-answer quality would push toward sameness; a set-level term is needed if ideation is optimised.

source: Sankar and Sen (2024): operational definitions
finding: Definitions used: novelty is the divergence of an idea from existing ones; variety is the richness of diversity among ideas; fluency is the count in a fixed time. Quality is reduced to a 'meaningful' vote in the pilot.
numbers: Six groups of five designers, 20 minutes per arm, about 80 ideas per set, 12 sampled for the variety rating.
limits: Variety rated by Likert on a sample, not computed from a tree.
agent_relevance: Shows how the Shah metrics get simplified in practice: ratings replace the genealogy tree.

source: Carichon et al. (2026): fixation by brief type and attribute
finding: Product briefs gave the highest novelty and rarity but lower fluency and diversity; procedure briefs gave broader output; service briefs were most conventional. Surprising and negative attribute words raised novelty and rarity but lowered diversity.
numbers: Differences reported significant (tables in appendix). Llama perplexity median 70.26 versus mean 1803.32 (outliers).
limits: Automatic metrics only.
agent_relevance: Novelty and diversity trade off. Report both; do not optimise one alone.

source: Carichon et al. (2026): simple prompts versus method scaffolds
finding: Complex method prompts (C-K, SCAMPER) did not reliably beat simple ones. Authors link novelty to explicit words such as 'wild' or 'unconventional' and to asking the model to leave categories already used.
numbers: 25 prompts; method prompts all beat control in t-tests; AI-specific and brainstorming variants had the highest top-5 novelty and rarity.
limits: Wording is confounded with method structure.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap operator: list categories used, then demand ideas outside them, with code checking category overlap.

source: Park et al. (2026) MUTATE: ideation profiles
finding: Models split into broad-ideation (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3-235B: many candidates but rotate inside one mechanism) and narrow-ideation (GPT-5.4, Llama 4). Breadth of candidates and discovery of a new mechanism are different skills.
numbers: Elaboration rose on all four models with ReDNA (GPT-5.4 2.827 to 3.262; Llama 2.667 to 3.021). EscapeAgent caused a large elaboration drop on Claude Sonnet.
limits: Per-family analyses are in an appendix I did not read.
agent_relevance: Counting ideas is not enough; count distinct mechanisms (Shah's working-principle level).

source: Schaeffer et al. (2026): inference-time fix
finding: Rebuts the claim that training-time change is needed. One sampler (min-p) failing does not show all inference-time methods fail; prompting reliably raises measured diversity.
numbers: Jiang reported 81% of pairs above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8 under min-p.
limits: Does not show prompting restores human-level spread.
agent_relevance: Keep inference-time diversity operators in scope; test each with a matched null.

source: Jiang et al. (2025): human rating gap
finding: LLMs, reward models and LM judges are less well calibrated to human ratings on outputs that split human raters, even at similar overall quality.
numbers: 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item.
limits: Taken from the abstract of the version read.
agent_relevance: A model judge of novelty is least reliable exactly where taste differs; use code-computed distances (G5).

source: Carichon et al. (2026) summary of reference-set practice (citing Fiorineschi and Rotini 2023, Grace 2015, Agogue 2014)
finding: Novelty and diversity are commonly operationalised as distance relative to a set of earlier solutions; defixation studies use a control group as the reference set.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Second-hand summary.
agent_relevance: Choose the reference set on purpose: our control pool is the same model with a plain prompt.

source: Human follow-ups to Shah (Nelson 2009; Linsey 2011; Sarkar and Chakrabarti 2011; Verhaegen 2013; Oman 2013)
finding: Only seen as names in reference lists (Sankar and Sen cite Nelson 2009 for diversity and Linsey 2011 for practicality). Their findings are not recorded here.
numbers: None.
limits: Gap: no primary human replication of the 2003 metrics was read this session; search APIs were rate limited and publisher pages blocked.
agent_relevance: Open item for a later pass: inter-rater reliability of novelty and variety ratings in human design studies.
